prompt: What is the main difference between the shop's PostgreSQL database and the warehouse Ana builds from it?
hint: Think about what each one is for.

choices.text: One records; the other answers questions
choices.why: Right. Same data, opposite designs: one for writing, one for reading.

choices.text: The warehouse holds data the tills never see, bought from outside suppliers
choices.why: No. The warehouse is loaded from the shop's database; the data is the same.

choices.text: The warehouse is a backup in case PostgreSQL fails
choices.why: No. A backup restores the same design; the warehouse is a different design.

choices.text: PostgreSQL is newer software
choices.why: No. The choice of engine is not the difference this course is about.

prompt: Why does the course recommend running its lab in a virtual machine?
hint: Look at what the setup installs and fills.

choices.text: DuckDB refuses to run outside a virtual machine
choices.why: No. DuckDB is one program and runs anywhere, including a browser.

choices.text: The data is too large for an ordinary laptop
choices.why: No. The programs, the database and the files come to under two gigabytes.

choices.text: A database server is easier to throw away than to remove
choices.why: Right. Deleting the virtual machine removes the server, its data and the packages in one go.

choices.text: PostgreSQL runs faster in a virtual machine than installed
choices.why: No. A virtual machine adds a layer; it does not speed anything up.

prompt: PostgreSQL keeps 89 MB of generated CSV files in about 1,100 MB. About how many times larger is the database than the files? Give a whole number.
hint: Divide the larger by the smaller.

prompt: After `ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_buffers = '512MB'`, `SHOW shared_buffers` still answers `128MB`. Why?
hint: When does the server read its configuration?

choices.text: The server reads that setting only when it starts
choices.why: Right. `sudo pg_ctlcluster 16 main restart`, and the same query answers 512MB.

choices.text: The role needs a password before it can change settings
choices.why: No. The four ALTER SYSTEM lines answered ALTER SYSTEM; the change was written.

choices.text: 512 MB is more memory than PostgreSQL 16 accepts
choices.why: No. It is a modest value, and after a restart the server uses it.

choices.text: The setting applies only to databases created afterwards
choices.why: No. It is a setting of the whole server, not of one database.

prompt: `psql` answers `FATAL: role "ana" does not exist`. What is missing?
hint: The server answered, so it is running.

choices.text: A PostgreSQL role with the login name, made by createuser
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu's PostgreSQL knows nobody until a role is created.

choices.text: The database shop, made by createdb
choices.why: No. That error names the database, and comes after the role exists.

choices.text: A running server, started with pg_ctlcluster
choices.why: No. A stopped server cannot say anything about roles.

choices.text: The generated files, written by generate.py
choices.why: No. psql never reads them; load.sh does, after the database exists.

prompt: The till asks for order 900001 by its number. What kind of question is that?
hint: How many orders does the question name?

choices.text: A question about many things over a period of time
choices.why: No. That describes the manager's report, which names no order at all.

choices.text: A question about one thing, now
choices.why: Right. One order, by its key, as it stands today.

choices.text: An analytical query that summarises a table
choices.why: No. Nothing is summarised; one order and its lines come back.

choices.text: A batch load from another system
choices.why: No. A load writes many rows; this reads one order.

prompt: Both the till's lookup and the manager's report are SQL against the same tables. What differs between them?
hint: The lesson says it is not difficulty.

choices.text: The report uses a different dialect of SQL
choices.why: No. Both ran in the same PostgreSQL, in the same SQL.

choices.text: The report is harder to write correctly
choices.why: No. The lesson's point is that they differ in shape, not difficulty.

choices.text: Only the till's lookup reads from an index
choices.why: True of these two plans, but it is a consequence of the shape, not the difference itself.

choices.text: Their shape: how many rows each touches, and whether it writes
choices.why: Right. A handful of rows now against every row summarised.

prompt: What does the T in OLTP stand for, and what is it?
hint: A unit of work that happens completely or not at all.

choices.text: Table: the unit everything in a relational database is stored in
choices.why: No. Both kinds of database have tables.

choices.text: Time: the moment a row was written
choices.why: No. Time matters more to the warehouse than to the till.

choices.text: Transaction: a small unit of work, all or nothing
choices.why: Right. Online transaction processing: many small transactions a second.

choices.text: Transfer: copying data from one system into another every night
choices.why: No. Copying between systems is what loads a warehouse.

prompt: How many 8 kB pages did PostgreSQL read to fetch order 900001 and its two lines?
hint: Add the two index scans.

prompt: `order_lines` grows from 900,000 lines to 9 million. What happens to the cost of fetching one order's lines by its number?
hint: How deep is a B-tree over a million keys?

choices.text: Almost nothing: one more tree level
choices.why: Right. The tree gets one level deeper for each large multiple of keys.

choices.text: It grows ten times, like the table it reads
choices.why: No. That would be a scan; a lookup walks the tree, not the table.

choices.text: It drops, because an index that is used more often stays in memory
choices.why: No. Use does not make a tree shallower.

choices.text: It doubles
choices.why: No. Nothing in a B-tree doubles with ten times the keys.

prompt: Which of these belong to the design of the shop's operational database? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what serves a till.

choices.text: A customer's city stored once, in `customers`
choices.why: Yes. Normalisation makes a change one `UPDATE` of one row.

choices.text: A foreign key refusing a line for a book that does not exist
choices.why: Yes. The bad row is refused while the person who typed it is still there.

choices.text: Every past city a customer lived in, kept in `customers`
choices.why: No. The row keeps the current value; the old one is overwritten.

choices.text: Totals by month precomputed for reports
choices.why: No. Nothing in the shop's schema serves a report.

prompt: The report's plan says `temp read=14555 written=14571`. What happened?
hint: Temporary files are written to disk.

choices.text: The report wrote its eight rows to a temporary table
choices.why: No. Eight rows are a few bytes; this is fourteen thousand pages.

choices.text: PostgreSQL read pages from another server
choices.why: No. There is one server in the lab.

choices.text: The cache was cold
choices.why: No. A cold cache shows as `read`, not as `temp`; the plan says `shared hit`.

choices.text: Part of the work did not fit in the memory one operation gets, so it went to disk and back
choices.why: Right. About 119 MB written to temporary files and read back.

prompt: The report needed five columns of `order_lines`. Why did PostgreSQL carry the others through memory as well?
hint: How does a row store lay data out?

choices.text: Because the query said `SELECT *`
choices.why: No. The query named its columns.

choices.text: Because it stores whole rows together, every column of a row on one page
choices.why: Right. To read one column of a row it reads the page holding the whole row.

choices.text: Because an index covered the other columns
choices.why: No. The report scanned the tables, not an index.

choices.text: Because the join needs every column to compare rows
choices.why: No. A join compares only its keys.

prompt: Match each trait to the workload it describes.
hint: One side writes all day; the other reads in large gulps.

pairs.left: Thousands of small writes a second
A total over millions of rows, grouped by a few columns
Data arriving in batches from other systems

prompt: A read replica takes the reports off the primary database. Which problem does it leave in place?
hint: What does the replica copy, exactly?

choices.text: The past it overwrote
choices.why: Right. The replica copies the same current-state rows, so the history is still gone.

choices.text: Reports slowing the tills down
choices.why: No. That is the one problem a replica solves.

choices.text: Reports reading data that is a whole night out of date
choices.why: No. A replica follows the primary a fraction of a second behind.

choices.text: The cost of a second licence
choices.why: No. PostgreSQL has no licence fee; and that is not what the lesson weighed.

prompt: A shop's reports run on its production database and take two seconds today. Why does the lesson expect the problem to get worse even if the shop does not grow?
hint: Compare what each workload reads in year five.

choices.text: Indexes slow down as they age
choices.why: No. Nothing in the lesson ages an index.

choices.text: The tills write more rows each year
choices.why: No. A shop that does not grow writes the same rows a day.

choices.text: The reports read the whole history, and it gets longer every month
choices.why: Right. The till's work is flat; the report's grows with every month kept.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a database to two years of data
choices.why: No. There is no such limit.

prompt: Why did the order lines keep the 2024 price of *The Salt Season IV* when `books` did not?
hint: What did the till write on each line?

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps old versions of every row
choices.why: No. Old row versions are cleaned away; the price on the line is a column.

choices.text: Each line recorded the price it was charged, at the moment of the sale
choices.why: Right. A fact recorded when it happened keeps its value.

choices.text: A trigger copied the old price into the lines when `books` changed
choices.why: No. There is no trigger; the price was written when the line was.

choices.text: The price rise was rolled back
choices.why: No. `books` shows the new price, R$ 159.90.

prompt: By how many reais did the price of *The Salt Season IV* rise between 2024 and 2025?
hint: Subtract the 2024 price from today's.

prompt: Customer 2123 moved from Minas Gerais to Paraná in April 2025. A report of 2024 sales by the customer's state is run against `customers`. Where are their 2024 orders counted?
hint: The row holds one state.

choices.text: In Minas Gerais, where the customer lived then
choices.why: That is the right answer to the question, and not what this report gives.

choices.text: Half in each state
choices.why: No. Nothing splits an order between states.

choices.text: Nowhere: the inner join drops them all
choices.why: No. The customer row exists, so the join keeps every order.

choices.text: In Paraná, where the row says
choices.why: Right. The join finds `PR`, whatever the date of the order.

prompt: A fact recorded at the moment it happened keeps its value. A description of something keeps only its ___ value.
hint: The opposite of the first one.

prompt: Which of Inmon's four properties says that the warehouse keeps the past?
hint: Every row knows the period it describes.

choices.text: Subject-oriented
choices.why: No. That is about organising by what the business asks about.

choices.text: Integrated
choices.why: No. That is about one definition across several sources.

choices.text: Time-variant
choices.why: Right. Every row belongs to a period, and the periods are kept.

choices.text: Non-volatile
choices.why: Close: it says rows are not edited by readers. Keeping each period is the next one.

prompt: The warehouse's query never mentions cancelled orders or how revenue is computed, and still gets the same totals as PostgreSQL. Why?
hint: When were those decisions made?

choices.text: They were decided once, when the warehouse was loaded
choices.why: Right. The fact table holds only valid sales, with revenue already computed.

choices.text: DuckDB filters cancelled orders by default
choices.why: No. DuckDB knows nothing about orders.

choices.text: The totals agree by coincidence
choices.why: No. Eight totals agreeing to the cent is not chance.

choices.text: The fact table is a copy of `order_lines` with nothing removed or computed
choices.why: No. Then cancelled orders would be counted and revenue would need computing.

prompt: PostgreSQL answered the report in 1,607.639 ms and the warehouse in 0.020 s. Roughly how many times faster was the warehouse? Give a whole number.
hint: Put both in milliseconds first.

prompt: Match each table of Ana's warehouse to what its rows are.
hint: `fact_` tables are events; `dim_` tables are context.

pairs.right: A book and what describes it

prompt: Which cost does the warehouse carry that it cannot design away?
hint: It is a copy.

choices.text: It needs the same indexes as the operational database
choices.why: No. It is designed for scans, and lesson 8 shows it needs few indexes.

choices.text: Its queries are slower than the operational database's
choices.why: No. The report ran eighty times faster there.

choices.text: It cannot keep history
choices.why: No. Keeping history is one of its jobs.

choices.text: It is only as fresh as its last load
choices.why: Right. A copy is as old as the moment it was made.

prompt: Match each need to what answers it.
hint: Each of the four solves a different part of the problem.

pairs.left: Reports slow the tills down, and nothing else is wrong
Every change to a row has to reach another system as it happens
Sales by the state the customer lived in at the time

prompt: Put these in the order a sale travels through Ana's systems, first to last.
hint: It is written before it is copied, and copied before it is read.
items: The till writes the order in PostgreSQL
The nightly load copies it into the warehouse
The manager's report reads it from the fact table
trap: A report run in the afternoon does not see the morning's sales: they reach the warehouse at the next load.

prompt: What does change data capture change about a warehouse?
hint: It reads the database's own log.

choices.text: Its model: facts and dimensions are no longer needed once every change streams in
choices.why: No. The lesson says CDC changes how it is loaded, not what it is.

choices.text: How it is loaded: continuously, with every intermediate state of a row
choices.why: Right. That includes the old city before an update, which makes it a rich source of history.

choices.text: Where it runs: on the primary database
choices.why: No. CDC streams the changes elsewhere.

choices.text: Nothing; it is another name for a replica
choices.why: No. A replica copies the current state; CDC delivers each change as an event.

prompt: A vendor says its HTAP database means the shop no longer needs a dimensional model. What is the strongest reply?
hint: Separate where the data sits from what it means.

choices.text: The pipeline goes; the model is about meaning, and a mover is still one row
choices.why: Right. History and shared definitions are needed wherever the data physically sits.

choices.text: HTAP databases are too slow for analysis
choices.why: No. They keep a columnar copy precisely so analysis is fast.

choices.text: HTAP stores every row twice, once by row and once by column, which doubles what the shop pays for storage
choices.why: A cost, perhaps, but it does not answer the claim about the model.

choices.text: A dimensional model is needed by law
choices.why: No. No law asks for one.

prompt: A product team wants a screen showing each customer's last five orders, refreshed as they buy. Where should it read from, and why?
hint: Apply the one-thing-now rule.

choices.text: The warehouse, because its columnar storage answers any query faster than PostgreSQL
choices.why: No. It is faster at scans; this is a lookup, and the warehouse is a night behind.

choices.text: A data lake
choices.why: No. Lesson 10's lake is for files at scale, not a per-customer screen.

choices.text: The operational database: one customer, now
choices.why: Right. A question about one thing now belongs to the operational side.

choices.text: Either; the data is identical
choices.why: No. The warehouse misses everything since its last load.

prompt: Ana is asked for "2024 revenue by the customer's region" and has only the operational database. What should she say about the numbers she can produce?
hint: Who moved?

choices.text: They are exact, because every order kept the customer it belonged to, whatever happened later
choices.why: The order kept the customer, not where the customer lived.

choices.text: The total is right; the split puts movers where they live now
choices.why: Right. 1,404 of the 2024 orders sit in a state their buyer had not moved to yet.

choices.text: Nothing can be produced until a warehouse exists
choices.why: No. A number can be produced; it needs its caveat.

choices.text: Both the total and the split are wrong
choices.why: No. Moving a customer moves no money; the total is unaffected.

prompt: Order these by how many 8 kB pages PostgreSQL touched for each, fewest first.
hint: One lookup, one full report and the spill to disk.
items: The report's pages read from memory
The report's pages written to temporary files
trap: The spill is larger than what was read from memory: 14,571 pages written against 12,518 hit.
